Title: We are invited, particularly in our developing countries, to restructure and enrich our financial landscape.

(04/11/2019 18:11:38) The Governor of the Central Bank of Mauritania (BCM), Mr. Abdel Aziz Ould Dahi, presented in Dakar the strategic vision of the BCM, aimed at introducing new technologies in financial services in Mauritania. The Governor was the distinguished guest of the International Conference organized by the BCEAO and the World Bank, on October 30 and 31, 2019, on the theme "FinTech: challenges, opportunities and prospects for developing countries". Following is the full speech of the Governor: The speech Governors, Ministers Distinguished participants, First of all, I would like to thank the BCEAO and the World Bank for organizing this high-level event and for involving us. The theme of this conference is, in my view, of great importance for inclusive development in our regionand in Africa as a whole. I have followed the following presentations with particular attention and, as a mere observer first of all, I draw a number of comments. First of all, I am struck by the great diversityof initiatives that have been presented. Undoubtedly, financial technology (FinTech) gives rise to new ideas and solicits innovations that offer wide opportunities! To the point that there are hardly any financial areas that do not seemto call for its deployment. I also note that, although recent, the appropriation of this technology by financial institutions has quickly translated into concrete applications, several of which have met with very encouraging success. Although "disruptive", as is often said, blockchain technology is nonetheless likely to find fairly immediate jobs. This shows that it is able to respond to real needs in our subregion. Finally, I am obviously sensitive to the advances in regulatory matters, to the accompanying mechanisms, such as sandboxes, which have been put in place and are being tested by the financial authorities. Certainly, questions remain. But we can only welcome the pragmatism deployed, to avoid any penalizing decoupling between what technology quickly makes possible to envisage and what regulation allows. From all this, as Governor of the Central Bank of Mauritania this time, I retain several decisive elements: First, if there is an innovative technology, open to a wide range of applications, we must take into account that its appropriation and implementation will be collective. Because, developing financial technology and, more broadly, digital finance, requires a whole "ecosystem". This means reciprocal contributions and cross-fertilization between different actors: banks and financial institutions, insurance companies and fintech startups, whose growth must be promoted. Obviously, regulators are an integral part of this ecosystem. Secondly, in the financial sphere, no one alone will be able to cover all the possible solutions, nor will they be able to envisage all the implications and risks, nor will they be able to mobilise the necessary resources and expertise. Finally, it will not only be a question of managing a technological transition. Rather, we are invited, particularly in our own countries, to recomposeand expand our financial landscape. This is why the involvement of regulatory authorities is essential, to both boost and supervise the evolution of a financial environment that will experience many impulses. This iswhy fintech must be seen as a farm of new requirements, which will become as general as they are pressing. Because it makes possible, in fact, more transparency and security, more traceability, reduced costs and secure document preservation, the use of blockchain will make these criteria more and more commonly demanded by the public. And this in many areas: the real innovation will be there, and it will be far from being limited to the finest spherealone. The financial sphere which, through the management of guarantees, in particular, invites to direct, at the national level, the use of the blockchain for the protection of individual data and the management of personal identities, as well as patrimonial and cadastral situations. While, at the same time, we will see  we have already seen it in fact  appear blockchain solutions for the administration and monitoring of logistics, food and health supply chains. New requirements will thus generate impetus in many areas. And the question that the regulator must ask itself is whether all these developments will be able to share common objectives. Because it will promote both their developmentand the support that can be given to them. I note in this sense that, as far as the financial sphere is concerned, the ecosystem that is likely to appear around digital finance corresponds to a landscape - particularly banking - more complete, more competitive, with expanded offers and more efficient services. In short, what is best able to promote financial inclusion! Financial inclusion, which is not limited to having a bank account, or even accessing credit. As defined by the UN, financial inclusion presupposes the existence and regulation of a complete and efficient financial system, offering economic agents a set of varied and cheap offers. And in the national framework for the fight against poverty, financial inclusion represents a decisive lever. The Central Bank of Mauritani e considers that it is fully responsible for exercising particular vigilance over the new technologies of digital finance and to promote both their appropriation and their development by economic actors, without replacing them. Thus, we see ourselves in a role of both tutor and spur and, to this end, we have launched a number of initiatives. These cover the evolution of the financial framework and its upgrading to international standards, as well as the development of digital payments. In addition, we carried out a first Fintech Challenge, last July, highlighting a large number ofMauritanian star tups, with cutting-edge skills and varied projects, which we want to support through a real Innovation Lab. Finally, seeking international expertise, we are exploring distributed ledger technology. And toabort its appropriation, we will launch a pilot application with microfinance institutions in our country. Also, we are about to update all the regulations relating to digital finance, to adopt a national sandbox and to launch a major digital payment portal project that will eventually allow the interoperability of all digital solutions on the market, particularly those relating to mobile payment, e-payment and other financial applications. This digital. Other initiatives will soon emerge, but this time from private financial or non-financial players, especially from startups with a strong technological connotation that already have promising prospects. All this finally leads me to underline  faced with the multiplicity of facets of digital finance and its applications, as well as the variety of skills that they mobilize  the importance of international exchanges, such as those that bring us together today. In warmly congratulating the organisers, I can only hope that such exchanges will be repeated and become frequent. Thank you.
